question: What is the primary instrument used during an otoscopic examination?
explanation: An otoscope is specifically designed with a light and magnifying lens to view the ear canal and eardrum. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why would you use an otoscope on a patient complaining of sudden ear pain?

options.A: To inspect the ear canal and eardrum for signs of inflammation or infection
options.B: To test the nerve pathways responsible for hearing sound
options.C: To flush out excess earwax blocking the inner ear
options.D: To measure the exact pressure inside the middle ear cavity

explanation: Ear pain often comes from a little trouble or infection in the canal. Using an otoscope lets you peek right in to see what's going on! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h1)

question: What color is a healthy, normal tympanic membrane?
explanation: A normal, healthy eardrum has a characteristic translucent, pearly-gray appearance. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h2)

question: How is the adult ear canal structured from outside to inside?

options.A: An outer bony section and an inner muscular section
options.B: An outer cartilaginous third and an inner bony two-thirds
options.C: A completely rigid tube made entirely of cartilage
options.D: An upper bony half and a lower cartilaginous half

explanation: The outer part of the ear canal is made of cartilage, while the deeper part sits right against the bone, which makes that inner area extra sensitive to touch. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the cone-shaped tip attached to the otoscope head called?
explanation: The speculum is the disposable or reusable cone attached to the otoscope that enters the ear canal. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h3)

question: When choosing a speculum size for an adult patient, what should you do?

options.A: Choose the largest size that fits comfortably into the ear canal
options.B: Select a pediatric size to ensure it does not touch the eardrum
options.C: Avoid using a speculum and insert the metal otoscope head directly
options.D: Always use the smallest size available to prevent patient discomfort

explanation: A bigger speculum actually keeps you from accidentally poking the instrument in too deep, while giving you a much better view! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h3)

question: How should you position an adult patient's pinna to straighten their ear canal before looking inside?
explanation: For adults, pulling the pinna upward and backward straightens out that natural S-curve of the ear canal so you can see clearly. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why do you straighten an infant's ear canal differently than an adult's?

options.A: Adult ear canals grow completely straight without any natural curves
options.B: An infant's ear canal is shorter and angled more horizontally
options.C: An infant's pinna is made entirely of hard, rigid bone
options.D: Infants cannot sit upright during any part of a physical assessment

explanation: Babies' ears are shaped a bit differently! Because their canals are shorter and flatter, you pull gently downward and back to get a good view. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why is it important to rest your fingers against the patient's cheek while holding the otoscope?

options.A: To block out bright room lighting for a clearer visual field
options.B: To prevent injury to the ear canal if the patient suddenly moves
options.C: To keep the otoscope battery handle from becoming disconnected
options.D: To warm up the speculum before it touches the sensitive skin

explanation: Bracing your hand on their cheek is a brilliant safety trick. If the patient jerks or moves, your hand moves with them, protecting the delicate ear canal! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h5)

question: When should you inspect the outside of the ear (the auricle)?

options.A: Only after the otoscopic examination is fully completed
options.B: While cleaning cerumen out of the middle ear space
options.C: Before inserting the speculum into the ear canal
options.D: Immediately after removing the pneumatic bulb attachment

explanation: Always check the outside of the ear first for any tenderness or sores before putting anything into the canal. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the bright triangular light reflex seen on a normal tympanic membrane called?
explanation: The cone of light is a normal light reflection bouncing off the concave surface of the healthy eardrum. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which landmark appears as a vertical streak running across the upper portion of the normal tympanic membrane?
explanation: The handle of the malleus is embedded in the eardrum and shows clearly as a streak extending down from the top edge. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h6)

question: What does a nurse typically see during an otoscopic exam of a patient with acute ear infection (otitis media)?

options.A: A clear, translucent eardrum with a sharp cone of light
options.B: A dark perforated hole with dry flaky skin inside the canal
options.C: A bulging, bright red tympanic membrane with obscured landmarks
options.D: A completely pale, flat membrane with prominent bone outlines

explanation: When pus builds up behind the eardrum from an infection, it pushes the drum outward and turns it very red, hiding the normal landmarks. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which finding means the external ear canal is completely blocked?
explanation: Cerumen impaction just means a buildup of earwax has packed tightly into the canal, blocking your view completely. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the most important infection control rule when examining multiple patients' ears?

options.A: Washing the entire otoscope handle in boiling water daily
options.B: Wiping only the lens of the otoscope between patients
options.C: Changing the disposable speculum for every single patient
options.D: Using alcohol swabs to clean the inside of the ear canal

explanation: Always use a fresh speculum for each patient to keep germs from spreading from one ear to another. Safety first! [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h8)

question: What essential details should you include in your nursing notes after an ear exam?

options.A: A detailed diagram of the patient's skull bones and cranial nerves
options.B: The appearance of the canal, eardrum color, landmark visibility, and any abnormal findings
options.C: The exact brand and serial number of the otoscope device used
options.D: Only the patient's reported hearing test scores from previous years

explanation: Good clinical notes always describe what you actually saw—like the color of the eardrum and whether landmarks were clear—so you can track the patient's healing. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T3#GNS221_U2_T3_h8)
